title: Where Does Return Air Go in an HVAC System?
h1: Where Does Return Air Go in an HVAC System, and Why Does It Matter?
description: Return vents pull room air back to the furnace or air handler to be filtered, heated or cooled. Here is how returns work and the signs of trouble.
quick_answer: A return air vent pulls air from your rooms back to the furnace or air handler. On the way, it passes through the filter, then gets heated or cooled and pushed back out through the supply vents. Without enough return air, the system can't move air properly, so rooms feel uneven and the equipment works harder.
body:
Your HVAC system is a loop. Supply vents blow conditioned air into the rooms, and return vents pull room air back to the equipment so it can be filtered and heated or cooled again. The return side is the half of the system most people never think about, but it decides how much air the whole system can move.

Where does return air go?

Air enters the return grille, travels through a return duct and reaches the return plenum, the box attached to the furnace or air handler. It passes through the filter, then the blower pushes it across the heat exchanger or cooling coil and out into the supply ducts.

In many Southern California homes, the equipment sits in the attic, the garage or a hall closet. In a lot of older stucco tract homes, the return is a single large grille in the hallway ceiling or a wall near the center of the house. Newer or larger homes often have several returns, sometimes one in each bedroom.

How can I tell a return vent from a supply vent?

A few quick clues:

  • Size. Returns are usually bigger than supply registers.
  • Louvers. Returns usually have fixed slats with no adjustable damper. Supply registers often have movable fins or a lever.
  • A filter behind the grille. If the grille swings open and holds a filter, it's a return.
  • The tissue test. With the system running, hold a tissue near the grille. If it gets pulled toward the grille, it's a return. If it blows away, it's a supply.

Why does return air matter so much?

A system can only push out as much air as it can pull back in. When the return side is too small, blocked or leaky, several things happen:

  • Airflow drops, so rooms take longer to heat or cool.
  • The blower works harder and gets louder, often with a whistle at the grille.
  • The AC coil can get too cold and freeze up.
  • A furnace can overheat and shut itself off on its safety limit.
  • Leaks in the return duct pull in dusty attic or garage air, which goes straight into the system after the filter.

That last point is a common cause of dusty homes and fast-clogging filters. When a return duct in the attic has a gap or a torn connection, it can draw in insulation fibers and fine attic dust.

Why do bedrooms with closed doors feel stuffy?

When a home has one central return, closing a bedroom door cuts that room off from it. The supply vent keeps pushing air in, but the air has no easy way out. The room becomes slightly pressurized, airflow slows, and it ends up warmer in summer and cooler in winter than the rest of the house.

There are a few common fixes:

  1. Leave doors open or cracked when you can.
  2. Make sure there's a gap under the door so air can pass.
  3. Add a transfer grille or a jumper duct that links the bedroom to the hallway.
  4. Add a dedicated return to the room.

Is it OK to block a return vent?

No. Blocking a return with furniture, rugs or storage boxes chokes the system. The same goes for closing off returns to "push" more air somewhere else. The system was sized to pull air through all of its returns, so closing one just makes the blower work harder.

Keep at least a foot or so of open space in front of each return and keep the grille clean. If the grille is dusty, vacuum it when you change the filter.

What are signs of a return air problem?

Watch for these:

  • A loud rush or whistle at the return grille
  • Doors that slam or drift when the system turns on
  • Filters that clog quickly or get sucked into the grille
  • Rooms that never get comfortable
  • Dust lines on carpet edges near walls and doors
  • An AC that ices up even with a clean filter

faqs: How many return vents should a house have?

It depends on the size of the house and the system. Many older homes get by with one central return, but larger homes and systems often need more than one. A technician can measure airflow and static pressure to tell whether your return is big enough.
Should a return vent be high or low on the wall?

Both can work. In Southern California, many returns are in hallway ceilings or high on walls, which helps pull warm air out in summer. What matters most is that the return is large enough, unobstructed and properly connected.
Can a dirty return vent cause problems?

A dusty grille cuts airflow a little, and a clogged filter behind it cuts airflow a lot. That can make the system run longer, freeze the AC coil or trip the furnace safety limit. Clean the grille and change the filter on schedule.
Why is my return vent so loud?

A noisy return usually means it's too small for the system or the filter is too restrictive or clogged. Air speeds up to squeeze through, which makes a rushing or whistling sound. Try a fresh filter first, then have the return sized if the noise continues.
